notes: Hand-picked, because eBird Status & Trends marks most Cambodian birds as rare and the automatic cut gives very few species. The list uses GBIF/eBird record counts (November 2026) as a ranking signal plus birding knowledge, and covers what a visitor on a normal 2 to 3 week trip meets: Angkor and Siem Reap, the Tonle Sap and Prek Toal (Spot-billed Pelican, Milky Stork, Greater and Lesser Adjutant, Painted Stork, Black-headed Ibis), Phnom Penh and the Mekong floodplain, Kampot, Kep and the coast, Mondulkiri and the Cardamom foothills, the Mekong at Kratie and Stung Treng (Mekong Wagtail, River Lapwing, River Tern, Great Thick-knee), and the northern plains at Tmatboey, Chhep and Kulen Promtep (Giant and White-shouldered Ibis, Sarus Crane, Bengal Florican, vultures), plus the common urban and farmland birds. Left out as rare, very local or needing special trips: vagrants, seabirds and boat trips, most winter ducks and rarer waders, most leaf warblers, bush warblers and other skulkers, most owls and nightjars, the pheasants and partridges of deep forest, and the very hard specialities (White-winged Duck, Masked Finfoot, Coral-billed Ground-Cuckoo, Germain's Peacock-Pheasant, Siamese Fireback). Cambodia has 3 endemic-status species in the database, all on this trip: the Cambodian Tailorbird (scrub along the Mekong and Tonle Sap floodplain, easy), the Cambodian Laughingthrush (Cardamom Mountains, mainly Phnom Aural, needs a guide) and the Cambodian Flowerpecker (Cardamom hills, also across the border in eastern Thailand). Left out for lack of usable photos in the library or because the photos could not be identified with confidence: Siamese Pied Starling (aspsta7, the photos on file show the white-cheeked Asian Pied Starling) and Hainan Blue Flycatcher (habfly1, the library's photos could not be told from other blue flycatchers). Cambodian Laughingthrush (camlau1) has only two usable card photos.
